extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, administrators and officials of unemployment insurance systems (UIC), tribunal chairs, and legislative drafters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended procedural/legislative standards to ensure effective claimant access, intervention, and participation in unemployment insurance decision-making, reviews, and tribunals. Covers office organization, evidence/monitoring of job search, pre- and post-decision intervention, tribunal practice, and legal-aid policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of labour market statistics as a criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The labour market statistics used by the UIC are compiled from job vacancies registered with the CMCs, private agencies and local newspapers, and are incomplete; nevertheless they constitute a valid criterion for deciding whether to make claimants subject to the 'Active Job Search Program'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution when using these statistics to evaluate a claimant's efforts: Agents should use supply figures only if they have comparable, recent statistics on demand. Use such statistics only as a guide and only when supply and demand data are comparable and recent; otherwise rely less on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give weight to local knowledge (Boards of referees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards of referees do not normally attach conclusive importance to compiled labour statistics, often preferring to rely on their own direct knowledge of the local labour market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preference is welcomed because Board members are selected partly on such local knowledge; local knowledge may be more reliable than incomplete central statistics for evaluating claimant efforts and local labour conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralization and office location to promote access
rubrics_metrics.description: Decentralized, small-scale type 3A offices (office manager, receptionist, service unit, BCO and claimants' files) are efficient and largely self-sufficient, facilitating claimant access to decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continue the trend to far-reaching decentralization, ideally to a network of self-sufficient type 3A offices organized into districts. Mitigate the danger of balkanization and unacceptable discrepancies by encouraging exchange of ideas and coordination at district/regional levels, energetic continuous monitoring at district level, and dynamic personnel management at regional level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalized service
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalized service is desirable and small-scale offices support personalized contact between claimant and identifiable Agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although full personalization (e.g., interview for every claimant) is impractical, personalize written correspondence (e.g., reply cards or short personal letters signed by the Agent responsible) to acknowledge receipt, announce processing and establish initial personal contact to reduce bureaucratic anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain specialist roles (BCOs vs Insurance Agents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of Benefits Control Officers (BCOs) and Insurance Agents differs in nature, tempo and methods, justifying two separate specialist officer categories and the retention of distinct functions (investigation and adjudication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid total integration of BCOs into service units; maintain their investigative role and keep them somewhat outside the unit structure while ensuring close co-operation between units and BCOs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits on personalization of processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Totally personalized service (e.g., interview every claimant) cannot be achieved given public habits and UIC capacity; at least one-third of claims will be processed by mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize practical limits but seek to personalize correspondence and initial contacts for mail-processed claims to maintain engagement and identity of responsible Agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active Job Search Program application criteria and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimants are made subject to the 'Active Job Search Program' selectively, typically if there is particular demand for their occupation in the area of residence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider applying the program more broadly: require all claimants to produce a list of attempts beginning the week before expiry of the 'reasonable interval' in sec.40(3) of the Act, summon them to an interview shortly thereafter, and then require periodic lists at intervals—this would verify search scope and allow provision of advice to expand searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for evidencing and monitoring job-search efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible methods include continuous compulsory lists (e.g., fortnightly reporting), spot-checks of randomly selected claimants, and selective monitoring (the chosen 'Active Job Search Program').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective monitoring was balanced and wise, but consider extensions. Ideally compel claimants to maintain lists of attempts (with employer statements where possible), use spot-checks to verify, and require lists/interviews at key points (e.g., expiry of reasonable interval).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and correctness of regulatory language on efforts requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Tergiversations in the French version of the regulation (reg.145(9) → sec.55(8)) created confusion over whether claimants must make 'some' reasonable efforts or 'all' customary and reasonable efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amend the French text to remove ambiguity (substitute definite article 'les' for indefinite 'des') so it clearly requires all efforts which a diligent and prudent person would customarily and reasonably be expected to make; follow the interpretation favored by the Ricard decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limitations of CMC registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration with Canada Manpower Centres (CMCs) is generally compulsory but, by itself, is not sufficient for claimants to find work because of operational limitations of CMCs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question the value of compulsory registration unless CMCs are properly resourced; improve CMC function as job bank by obliging employers to notify vacancies and giving CMCs resources to perform their role effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to be heard before decision (investigative contacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent direct contacts (telephone/interviews) between Insurance Agent and claimant normally warn the claimant that a decision is imminent; benefit-control interviews give the claimant an opportunity to present his version of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow third parties to assist claimants at benefit-control interviews to help assert their point of view; do not convert the BCO's investigative interview into a debate over decisions—BCO should establish facts and recommend, not adjudicate; however, ensure claimants are aware of administrative/criminal sanctions for false statements (preferably via summons letter reminding them of consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: BCO disclosure of 'draft decisions' — avoid turning investigation into debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Compelling BCOs to advise claimants of reasons for disqualification or draft decisions they will recommend to Agent II could lead to arguments and is inconsistent with their investigatory role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require BCOs to notify claimants of draft recommendations to preserve their fact-finding role and avoid intra-agency arbitration; maintain separation between investigator and decision-maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to re-examination after decision (sec.102) and statutory recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Sec.102 allows amendment of decisions 'on presentation of new facts or on being satisfied that the decision was given without knowledge of, or was based on a mistake as to, some material fact' and this review avenue is not subject to any time limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally incorporate the practice of automatic re-examination upon receipt of an appeal into procedural rules or statutes (e.g., require written appeal with grounds and mandate Commission review and notification of any amendments); propose explicit regulatory wording (e.g., proposed reg.179) to regularize the practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: File summary provision and timing before Board of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: The submission is currently forwarded about one week before the hearing; proposal to replace it with a comprehensive 'summary of the file' prepared within two weeks of appeal filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make preparation of the 'summary of the file' mandatory within two weeks of appeal filing and require it to be written at least one week prior to the hearing so claimants have adequate time to familiarize and prepare their defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimant's right and timing to apply for hearing before Board (reg.180 amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Current practice: claimant must apply for a hearing when filing appeal but Boards often accept late requests; proposal to amend reg.180 to permit application at any time before Board decision and set seven-day limits in certain referred/appealed cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amend regs so (1) claimant may apply at any time before the Board gives its decision when appealing under sec.94, and (2) apply seven-day limits where a claim is referred or appealed by an employer, aligning practice with the spirit of the Act and existing Board practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage attendance and representation prior to Board hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Pamphlet recommends claimants attend hearings or arrange representation; clerks and Agents II should reiterate this to claimants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clerks compiling hearing rolls should telephone claimants to urge attendance or representation; ensure claimants are aware and encouraged to participate to improve outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of power to summon parties and witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Chairmen of Boards of referees and Umpires make too little use of powers to summon claimants or third-party witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chairmen should more actively summon parties and witnesses when appropriate; better advance planning and quicker file processing would assist in making effective use of summons powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate hearing time allocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal hearing length was set at half an hour; exceptions for labour disputes allocate several hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate half an hour for appeals where appellant does not appear, one hour where appellant is confirmed to appear, and several hours for labour disputes; allow additional time for deliberation and decision-writing so cases are not rushed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit UIC officials from being present during tribunal deliberations
rubrics_metrics.description: The UIC prohibits its officials (including clerks) from taking part in or being present during Board deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uphold this fundamental litigation principle strictly: violations are rare but would constitute sufficient grounds to invalidate Board decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamline re-examination procedure via chairman's preliminary determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically it is difficult to reconvene the same referees for re-examination under sec.102, creating confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the chairman of the original Board power to make a non-appealable determination whether facts presented are new or material or whether there was a mistake; only if chairman recognizes such grounds should the Board reconvene with same composition to decide merits—proposed statutory/regulatory amendments provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedite Umpire pre-hearing processing to maintain claimant participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Slowness in processing files and delays before Umpire hearings reduce the practical interest and deter claimant participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward files more quickly to the Umpire and enable Umpires to devote more time to pre-hearing planning so they can decide on summonses and better manage hearings; expedite pre-hearing procedure to incentivize appellant appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal time limits for requesting Umpire hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reg.185 (3) and (4) allow the public fifteen days from docket filing while the UIC can wait until decision has been given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a uniform fifteen-day period for all potential appellants and intervening parties (including the UIC) to request hearings before the Umpire, aligning time limits with reg.184(5) for filing representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply informality principle broadly to enhance participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sec.93(1) embodies a principle of informality for hearings before the Umpire and tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply informality as widely as possible: reduce legal formalities to the indispensable minimum because unnecessary formality inhibits uninitiated claimants and is detrimental to their cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal aid and representation policy for claimants
rubrics_metrics.description: Various organizations providing legal aid have overall positive effects; experts on claimant's side appear to increase chances before Boards of referees, but presence of an expert is not decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote increased personal participation by claimants rather than greater expert intervention. Do not create a system of automatic legal aid for all appellants; avoid UIC providing in-house legal aid to all claimants (would lack credibility). Legal aid should remain targeted and not undermine responsible public participation.
